summary:
A trans visitor to Idaho stands under the United States federal framework in every respect concerning documents and entry. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already carrying an X remain valid until expiry. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the changed treatment of trans passports to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Idaho's own statute is the sharper exposure on the ground. House Bill 752 was signed by the governor and takes effect on 1 July 2026. It makes it a crime for a trans person to use a restroom or changing room that does not match their sex in government buildings and in public-facing private businesses, including gas stations, restaurants, entertainment venues and hospitals. A first offence is a misdemeanour carrying up to a year in jail.

According to the ACLU, House Bill 752 is the only state law in the country extending bathroom criminalisation to private businesses, and it carries steeper penalties than other states' bans. Six transgender Idahoans filed suit on 30 April 2026, before the 1 July effect date, arguing that the measure is unconstitutional. The ACLU's filing asserts due-process, equal-protection and privacy violations and notes that the law targets no actual criminal conduct. National wire reporting covered the legislature's passage of the ban and the jail penalties it carries, along with a lawsuit that has partially blocked it.

A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest "Do Not Travel" state for trans people, bringing the total to four states so flagged, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends.
tangentialFactors:
Idaho's statute sits inside a national pattern rather than standing alone. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states; 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban, and some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances.

Enforcement under comparable laws has produced arrests. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.

Facilities exposure compounds at the federal layer. Executive Order 14168 barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, so a visitor may face both Idaho's criminal rule in state buildings and the federal restriction in federally funded settings.

Entry screening carries an outing risk independent of Idaho law. TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy. Several foreign governments responded to US document and data rules: in April 2025 CNN reported that several countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States, and Axios reported in March 2025 that at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the US.

Visa screening carries its own exposure. In February 2025 the State Department announced a ban on trans athletes entering the US to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent ban on grounds of fraud.

Care access is constrained for visitors who need it. Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," some hospitals paused care, and in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for records of patients under 19. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is already banned in 27 states. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.
localsOnly:
House Bill 752 applies to Idaho residents in the same terms as to visitors: use of a restroom or changing room inconsistent with sex in a government building or a public-facing private business is a criminal offence, and a first offence carries up to a year in jail. The list of covered private premises includes gas stations, restaurants, entertainment venues and hospitals, so ordinary daily errands are covered by the prohibition rather than only public facilities.

The ACLU of Idaho filed suit on 30 April 2026 arguing due-process, equal-protection and privacy violations, and noting that the law targets no actual criminal conduct. Six transgender Idahoans are the named challengers, and their complaint argues that House Bill 752 is unconstitutional. National wire reporting covered the legislature's passage of the ban alongside the litigation that has partially blocked it.

The measure's reach to private businesses and its penalty level distinguish it from bathroom statutes in other states: the ACLU describes it as the only state law extending bathroom criminalisation to private businesses, with steeper penalties than other states' bans.
outOfScopeNotes:
The scope of the partial block is unresolved here. National wire reporting states that a lawsuit partially blocked House Bill 752, but the inventory does not identify which provisions are stayed, which geographic areas the order covers, or whether it was in force on the 1 July 2026 effective date. Visitors should verify current status directly with the ACLU of Idaho before travel.

Idaho-specific rules on changing sex markers on birth certificates and driver's licences are not sourced in this inventory. Whether Idaho has followed states such as Kansas, which in February 2026 enacted a law preventing trans people from changing markers and invalidating existing mismatched documents, is unresolved rather than confirmed either way.

Enforcement practice under House Bill 752 is not documented in the inventory: there is no reported count of charges, arrests or complaints, and no source on how private businesses are expected to identify or report users.

The July 2026 "Do Not Travel" designation is a risk-assessment finding from a national assessment rather than a government order, and its methodology is not reproduced here.
